title: Abdominal Pain
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman with recent appendectomy who presents to the inpatient unit with RLQ abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting. She is febrile and tachycardic with localized RLQ tenderness. Labs show leukocytosis. The combination of recent abdominal surgery, fever, tachycardia, and localized pain is highly suggestive of a postoperative intra-abdominal abscess. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is the imaging of choice. Management involves percutaneous image-guided abscess drainage (first-line, avoiding the morbidity of open laparotomy) plus broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics covering gram-negative organisms, anaerobes, and enterococci.
chief_complaint: RLQ abdominal pain, fever, nausea post-appendectomy

stacks.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
stacks.finding: Determine how sick the patient looks.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
stacks.finding: Investigate for lung pathology — sometimes presents as abdominal pain.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
stacks.finding: Investigate for cardiac pathology. Tachycardia noted.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
stacks.finding: Chief complaint — RLQ tenderness, assess for peritoneal signs.

stacks.label: Bacterial culture, blood
stacks.finding: Fever + tachycardia after abdominal surgery is concerning — blood culture warranted prior to antibiotics.

stacks.label: Bacterial culture, urine
stacks.finding: Abdominal pain — urine culture to rule out GU pathology prior to antibiotics.

stacks.label: CBC with differential
stacks.finding: Important in febrile patient. Leukocytosis supports infection.

stacks.label: Chest X-ray
stacks.finding: Lung pathology can present as abdominal pain — rule out.

stacks.label: Urinalysis
stacks.finding: Rule out bacterial infection and other causes of fever.

stacks.label: Bacterial culture, abscess
stacks.finding: Culture of drained abscess confirms organism and guides antibiotic therapy.

stacks.label: Gram stain, abscess
stacks.finding: Gram stain provides early guidance for antibiotic selection before culture results.

stacks.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / LFTs
stacks.finding: Chemistries are important screening tool.

stacks.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast
stacks.finding: CT with IV contrast is preferred for abdominal pathology — will reveal intra-abdominal abscess.

stacks.label: Normal saline / Lactated Ringer
stacks.finding: Low sodium, nausea/vomiting — IV fluids indicated for resuscitation.

stacks.label: Analgesia (Hydromorphone / Fentanyl / Morphine / Ketorolac)
stacks.finding: Patient is in pain — treat. Nauseous, so IV route appropriate.

stacks.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Meropenem / Pip-Tazo / Cipro + Metronidazole / Cefepime + Metronidazole)
stacks.finding: Empiric antimicrobials with broad-spectrum activity against gram-negatives, anaerobes, and enterococci for high-severity community-acquired intra-abdominal infection.

stacks.label: Antiemetic (Ondansetron / Metoclopramide / Promethazine)
stacks.finding: Patient is nauseous — treat symptomatically.

stacks.label: Acetaminophen
stacks.finding: Patient is febrile. Ibuprofen/NSAIDs not ideal after recent surgery and upcoming procedure.

stacks.label: Needle drainage, abscess, imaging guided
stacks.finding: First step: percutaneous image-guided drainage. Avoids difficult laparotomy, anesthesia, wound complications, and reduces hospitalization length. Open laparotomy is excessive — less invasive first.

stacks.label: Intravenous access
stacks.finding: Good practice for IV fluids/medications.

stacks.label: Advise patient, safe sex techniques
stacks.finding: Patient is sexually active — review safe sex practices.

stacks.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
stacks.finding: One of the most important health interventions — excellent opportunity.

stacks.label: Papanicolaou smear / HPV DNA test
stacks.finding: Patient has not had recent pap smear — should be scheduled.

physical_exam.abdominal: RLQ tenderness. Assess for rebound, guarding. Post-surgical setting — concern for abscess.

decoys.label: Open laparotomy (first-line)
decoys.reason_wrong: Percutaneous drainage is preferred — less invasive, avoids laparotomy morbidity, reduces hospitalization. Open only if percutaneous approach fails or necrotic tissue present.

decoys.label: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/ketorolac)
decoys.reason_wrong: Patient recently had surgery and needs another procedure — increased bleeding risk. Acetaminophen preferred for fever.

decoys.label: Discharge from ED
decoys.reason_wrong: Intra-abdominal abscess requires inpatient monitoring. Percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + observation.

teach_me_steps.reasoning: CT with contrast is imaging of choice for intra-abdominal pathology. Reveals abscess, characterizes location for drainage planning.

teach_me_steps.order: Blood and urine cultures BEFORE antibiotics
teach_me_steps.reasoning: Cultures obtained prior to antibiotics maximize pathogen identification. Post-surgical fever + tachycardia warrants blood cultures.
First-line for accessible abscess without necrotic tissue. Less invasive than laparotomy, reduces length of stay.
Cover gram-negatives, anaerobes, enterococci. Pip-tazo, meropenem, or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole.
Post-procedural monitoring required. IV antibiotics, drain management, observation for clinical improvement.

case_summary: Post-appendectomy intra-abdominal abscess. Recent surgery + RLQ pain + fever + tachycardia + leukocytosis. CT shows abscess → percutaneous drainage + broad-spectrum antibiotics + IV fluids + inpatient monitoring. Prevention: smoking cessation, safe sex counseling, pap smear.
